title: A Standard Quantum Mechanical Treatment to Rationalize the Delayed-Choice Quantum Eraser
authors: Vipul Badhan, Pranvi, Samreet Dhillon, Bindiya Arora
abstract: Ever since the proposal of delayed choice quantum erasure and subsequent realization in the experiment by Kim et al., the interpretation and implications of delayed-choice experiments have remained a subject of intense foundational debate. This paper resolves the apparent paradox attached to the experiment using standard quantum mechanics. Using an extended Mach-Zehnder interferometer which captures every operational feature of the original experiment, we show that choosing between which-path and erasure detectors is simply a choice of measurement bases, which does not rewrite a photon's past. Furthermore, by mapping the experiment to a two-way Stern-Gerlach framework, we prove that quantum erasure is an expected result of measuring entangled states, not a physical anomaly. Ultimately, through a pedagogical game, we illustrate that the illusion of retrocausality arises from asking illegitimate questions, and that a forward-in-time description is entirely sufficient to explain the logic.
summary: This paper resolves the paradoxes of the delayed-choice quantum eraser by showing that the choice between measurement types is merely a selection of measurement bases within standard quantum mechanics. By modeling the system with an extended MZI and entangled pairs, the authors demonstrate that interference patterns are fully explained without invoking retrocausality. The work emphasizes that apparent paradoxes stem from conceptual misunderstandings about time and causality in quantum theory.
main_problem: To resolve the apparent paradoxes associated with delayed-choice quantum eraser experiments using standard quantum mechanics, specifically addressing the illusion of retrocausality.
main_result: The choice between which-path and erasure detectors is shown to be equivalent to choosing measurement bases, proving that quantum erasure is an expected result of measuring entangled states within a forward-in-time framework.
method: The analysis uses standard quantum mechanical formalism applied to an extended Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) setup involving entangled photon pairs.
model_or_system: The core system is the MZI, modeled with an Entangled Photon-Pair Source (EPPS), which allows tracking correlations between signal and idler paths. The analysis maps the experiment to a two-way Stern-Gerlach framework for conceptual clarity.
key_observables: Interference patterns (constructive/destructive) observed at various detectors, joint detection probabilities for coincident clicks in different measurement bases.
important_parameters: The beam splitter parameter $	heta$ controls the operational regime of the setup, allowing selection between path-erasure ($	heta=0$), which-way ($	heta=\pi$), and delayed choice ($	heta=\pi/2$).
main_assumptions: The approach relies on standard quantum mechanics formalism and assumes lossless operation of optical components; it explicitly avoids retrocausal frameworks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MZI setup, showing interference conditions for different path choices. The paper also uses a ball-and-box game analogy to model the delayed choice correlation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing basic MZI behavior, then analyzing specific cases (path-erasure vs. which-way) using entangled pairs, culminating in a unified treatment of the delayed choice mechanism via basis selection.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical grounding for interpreting foundational quantum optics experiments, clarifying that apparent non-local effects are artifacts of ill-posed questions rather than violations of causality.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic representation of a standard beam splitter BS. Input spatial modes |a⟩and |b⟩undergo a unitary transformation, yielding output spatial modes |γ0⟩and |γ1⟩

FIG. 2: Standard Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI). An incident photon entering via input mode |a⟩is split by BS1 into spatial modes |γ0⟩and |γ1⟩. After reflection at mirrors M1 and M2 and undergoing a relative phase shift ϕ, the paths recombine at BS2. Output modes |d1⟩ and |d2⟩are registered by detectors D1 and D2, respectively.

FIG. 3: Extended MZI configuration with entangled photon pair sources (EPPS) situated along modes |γ0⟩ and |γ1⟩generate signal (|s0⟩, |s1⟩) and idler (|i0⟩, |i1⟩) modes. Signal modes recombine at BS2 leading to detectors D1 and D2. Idler modes undergo recombination at BS5 yielding output modes |d5⟩and |d6⟩registered by detectors D5 and D6. Coincidence detections between (D1, D5) and (D2, D6) highlight complementary anti-interference and interference sub-ensembles.

FIG. 4: Extended MZI configuration with idler modes |i0⟩and |i1⟩directed by mirrors M3 and M4 straight to detectors D3 (mode |d3⟩) and D4 (mode |d4⟩). A click at D3 or D4 provides path information for the corresponding signal photon at D1 or D2.

FIG. 5: Extended MZI obtained by replacing mirrors M3 and M4 in the case II with 50:50 beam splitters BS3 and BS4 unifies both operational modes (case I and case II) into a single schematic. Reflected idler modes (|d3⟩, |d4⟩) yield which-path measurements at detectors D3 and D4, while transmitted modes (|i′ 0⟩, |i′ 1⟩) recombine at BS5 for erasure measurements at D5 and D6. Arbitrarily extending the idler optical path lengths ensures signal registration at D1/D2 strictly precedes the idler measurement choice.
